title: Calculations
description: Eight calculations of the lab and of physiology: magnification, dilutions, cell counts, flow and resistance, time constants and the Nernst equation.
instructions:
Eight questions, each answered with a number. Type the number only: the units are shown next to the box.

  • You can type powers of ten as 1.5 × 10^6, 1.5x10^6 or 1.5e6, and negative numbers with a minus sign.
  • The calculator is at the top of the page. You can move it by its title bar, and it remembers its last answer (Ans).
  • Answers are checked when you have submitted: the review shows the worked answer to each question.

questions.title: Calibrating an eyepiece graticule
questions.text:
An eyepiece graticule is calibrated with a stage micrometer at one objective: 25 eyepiece units line up exactly with 100 µm on the stage micrometer.

With the same objective, a cell is 6 eyepiece units across. How wide is the cell, in µm?
questions.guidance:
One eyepiece unit = 100 µm ÷ 25 = 4 µm at this objective.

The cell is 6 × 4 µm = 24 µm across.

The calibration has to be done again for each objective, because the stage micrometer looks larger at a higher magnification while the graticule (in the eyepiece) does not.

questions.title: Real size from the magnification
questions.text:
An electron micrograph was taken at a magnification of ×25 000. A mitochondrion is 50 mm long in the micrograph.

What is its real length, in µm?
questions.guidance:
Real size = size in the image ÷ magnification = 50 mm ÷ 25 000 = 0.002 mm.

0.002 mm × 1000 µm/mm = 2 µm.

questions.title: Making a dilution
questions.text:
You need 50 mL of 0.15 M NaCl, and you have a stock solution of 2.0 M NaCl.

What volume of the stock solution do you need, in mL? (You make it up to 50 mL with water.)
questions.guidance:
C1V1 = C2V2, so V1 = C2V2 ÷ C1 = (0.15 M × 50 mL) ÷ 2.0 M = 3.75 mL.

Check: the stock is 2.0 ÷ 0.15 ≈ 13.3 times more concentrated than you need, and 50 mL ÷ 13.3 ≈ 3.75 mL.

questions.title: Concentration after a dilution
questions.text:
You add 20 µL of a protein solution at 5 mg/mL to 980 µL of buffer, and mix.

What is the concentration of the protein in the mixture, in µg/mL?
questions.guidance:
The final volume is 20 µL + 980 µL = 1000 µL, so the solution is diluted 1000 ÷ 20 = 50 times.

5 mg/mL ÷ 50 = 0.1 mg/mL = 100 µg/mL.

(Or with C1V1 = C2V2: C2 = 5 mg/mL × 20 µL ÷ 1000 µL = 0.1 mg/mL.)

questions.title: Counting cells with a haemocytometer
questions.text:
A cell suspension is mixed with an equal volume of trypan blue, and loaded into a haemocytometer. Each large square is 1 mm × 1 mm, and the chamber is 0.1 mm deep.

The unstained cells in the four large corner squares are counted: 52, 47, 55 and 46.

What is the concentration of live cells in the original suspension, in cells per mL? (You can type a power of ten as 1.5 × 10^6, 1.5x10^6 or 1.5e6.)
questions.guidance:
The mean count is (52 + 47 + 55 + 46) ÷ 4 = 200 ÷ 4 = 50 cells per large square.

One large square holds 1 mm × 1 mm × 0.1 mm = 0.1 mm³ = 1 × 10−4 mL, so the diluted suspension has 50 ÷ 10−4 = 5 × 105 cells/mL.

Mixing with an equal volume of trypan blue diluted the cells 2 times, so the original suspension has 5 × 105 × 2 = 1.0 × 106 cells/mL.

questions.title: Resistances in series and in parallel
questions.text:
Blood flows through an artery (resistance 2 mmHg·min/mL), then through two capillary beds that are side by side, in parallel (resistances 6 and 3 mmHg·min/mL), and then through a vein (resistance 1 mmHg·min/mL).

The pressure difference from the start of the artery to the end of the vein is 90 mmHg. What is the total blood flow, in mL/min?
questions.guidance:
Flow, pressure and resistance are related as current, voltage and resistance are in Ohm’s law: Q = ΔP ÷ R (Darcy’s law).

The two capillary beds in parallel: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6, so R = 2 mmHg·min/mL. (Resistances in parallel give less resistance than either one alone.)

In series, resistances add: Rtotal = 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 mmHg·min/mL.

Q = 90 mmHg ÷ 5 mmHg·min/mL = 18 mL/min.

questions.title: The time constant of a membrane
questions.text:
A cell membrane has a resistance of 50 MΩ and a capacitance of 200 pF.

What is the membrane time constant (τ = RC), in milliseconds?
questions.guidance:
τ = RC = (50 × 106 Ω) × (200 × 10−12 F) = 10 000 × 10−6 s = 1 × 10−2 s = 10 ms.

After one time constant, the membrane potential has gone 63% of the way to its new value after a step of current.

questions.title: An equilibrium potential
questions.text:
The concentration of K+ is 140 mM inside a cell and 5 mM outside.

Use the Nernst equation to work out the equilibrium potential for K+ at 37 °C, in mV. (R = 8.314 J K−1 mol−1, F = 96 485 C mol−1, 0 °C = 273 K.)
questions.guidance:
E = (RT ÷ zF) × ln([K+]out ÷ [K+]in), with T = 310 K and z = +1.

RT ÷ F = (8.314 × 310) ÷ 96 485 = 0.0267 V = 26.7 mV.

ln(5 ÷ 140) = ln(0.0357) = −3.33.

E = 26.7 mV × −3.33 = −89 mV (inside negative). Answers from −88 to −90 mV are accepted.

The shortcut at 37 °C is E = 61.5 mV × log10([K+]out ÷ [K+]in) for an ion with one charge.
